instruments.label: Radius astronomicus (cross-staff) — the student instrument
instruments.description: The cross-staff (radius) of Tycho's student years at Leipzig and Rostock. With it, observing the 1563 great conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter, he found both the Alphonsine and Copernican tables badly in error — the observation that set his life's programme. He later moved decisively beyond such medieval portable instruments (astrolabe, torquetum, cross-staff) toward the large fixed quadrant, sextant and armillary of the ancients. Not extant.
instruments.principle: Sight from the end of the long graduated staff to both ends of a sliding cross-piece; slide the cross-piece until the two sight-lines just bracket the two targets, then read the subtended angle off the staff (directly, or via a tangent table). A shorter cross-piece is swapped in for small angles.
instruments.attested_by: Tycho's own account of his student years, appended to the Mechanica (1598): a wooden radius he had made in 1564 after Gemma Frisius's design (trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946).

instruments.label: Quadrans maximus — the great Augsburg quadrant
instruments.material: oak, iron-bound, with a brass-faced limb
instruments.dimensions: radius at least 14 cubits — Tycho's own figure, ≈543 cm (≈5.5 m) (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 20, p. 89)
instruments.fate: destroyed in a great storm, December 1574
instruments.description: A quadrant of c.5.5 m radius (at least 14 cubits in Tycho's own figure), so large it needed some twenty men to raise, built 1569–70 in Paul Hainzel's garden at Göggingen near Augsburg — the earliest of Tycho's monumental instruments. Destroyed in a storm in December 1574. In his own words: “I think that I will also add a delineation and description of the great quadrant which we had constructed 26 years ago in Master Paul Hainzel's garden on his property half a mile from Augsburg, although it does not exist any more.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 89).
instruments.location: Paul Hainzel's garden, Göggingen, near Augsburg
instruments.accuracy: scale divided to 1′ (≈1.6 mm per arcminute on the 5.5 m arc)
instruments.principle: A 90° arc hung from its centre with a plumb-line. Turned in azimuth and its edge brought onto the star, the plumb-line cuts the arc and splits the right angle into the zenith distance (above) and the altitude (below): h = 90°−z.

instruments.label: Quadrans muralis sive Tichonicus — the great mural quadrant
instruments.material: brass arc on a meridian wall
instruments.dimensions: radius nearly five cubits — Tycho's own figure, ≈194 cm (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 5, p. 29, in the editors' conversion); Wolfschmidt 2002 gives 194 cm; Thoren's 'two metres' is a rounding.
instruments.fate: the Hven instruments destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: A brass arc fixed to a wall set precisely in the meridian (north–south) at Uraniborg — Tycho's most celebrated instrument. Radius 194 cm — Tycho's own 'nearly five cubits' (Wolfschmidt 2002, p. 207; Thoren's 'two metres' is a rounding). Planned from 1576 and emerging from his Hven shop in June 1582 (Thoren, p. 163); Tycho was still adjusting it on the wall in 1583 (Thoren, p. 164 fn 43). Limb five inches broad, two inches thick — Tycho's own figures (Raeder 1946, p. 28), roughly 8 × 3 cm by Thoren's own conversion (arc breadth = 1/24 of the five-cubit radius; p. 163 n. 42). Thoren's main-text 'thirteen millimeters broad, and five millimeters thick' (p. 163) contradicts his own footnote and is an error. The wall within the arc bore the famous triple mural painting of Tycho himself amid views of Uraniborg's chambers. Its transversal scale was graduated to sixths of a minute; only after 1585, when the great armillary and the revolving quadrant became available to check its results, did Tycho regard its positions as confirmed (Thoren, p. 190). Known from the Mechanica engraving. In his own words: “It is called Mural, or Tichonicus, after the wall on which it is fixed. … every single minute can be divided again into six subdivisions; thus ten seconds of arc are plainly distinguishable and even half this, or five seconds of arc, can be read without difficulty.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 29).
instruments.location: south-west ground-floor room, Uraniborg (fixed on the meridian wall)
instruments.principle: A quarter-circle fixed flat on a wall set exactly in the meridian, its centre at a sight-cylinder through the south wall, graduated 0° at the top down to 90° on the plumb-line. Because the altitude and the arc above the sight-line are equal vertical angles, and the scale starts from the top, the reading is the meridian altitude directly.
instruments.image_credit: Tycho Brahe, Astronomiæ instauratæ mechanica (Wandsbek, 1598). Det Kongelige Bibliotek, Copenhagen, LN 432 2°, copy 2 (Nielsen 432). Public domain.

blaeu.context_title: Interior of Uraniborg with the mural quadrant in use — the most famous image in the atlas
blaeu.observatory: South wall of the main building, Uraniborg
blaeu.english:
THE MURAL QUADRANT OF TYCHO.

Blaeu describes the great mural quadrant painted on the south wall of Uraniborg's main building. Radius ca. 6 feet; graduated to one-sixth of a minute by transversal dots. Three assistants are used simultaneously: one calls the star name, one reads the altitude from the scale, one records the time from the clock — as depicted in the famous interior view (p. 201), which Blaeu reproduces as a coloured engraving from the Astronomiae Instauratae Mechanica (Wandsbek, 1598). At the arc's centre, Tycho placed a self-portrait as part of the wall painting — an instrument that was also his grandest act of self-fashioning.

instruments.label: Brass azimuthal quadrant
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: An early brass quadrant mounted to turn in azimuth, among the first instruments of the Hven period (1576). Not extant. In his own words: “Therefore I generally refer to this as the portable azimuth quadrant.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 22).

instruments.accuracy: read to ≈1′ (neither Nonius nor transversal on this one)
instruments.principle: A brass altitude-azimuth quadrant on a horizontal circle: swing in azimuth onto the body, slide the alidade onto it to read altitude on the arc, and read the bearing on the azimuth circle — altitude and azimuth together. Light enough to dismount for travel.

instruments.label: Revolving quadrant (quadrans azimuthalis volubilis)
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: A large revolving wood quadrant — 'one-and-a-half-meter' per Thoren (p. 177), 155 cm per Wolfschmidt 2002 — available at the turn of 1585–6 (Thoren, p. 177). Probably an experimental analogue to the mural quadrant, kept rigid by lightweight struts instead of anchors to a wall, so it could be turned to any azimuth. Together with the great equatorial armillary it gave Tycho the redundancy to verify his mural quadrant systematically, enabling the 1′ accuracy milestone achieved by the 1585 comet season. The second large quadrant (the revolving steel quadrant) entered service two years later. Not extant. In his own words: “A revolving quadrant, which can be used for determining not only altitudes, like the previous sextant, but also, most accurately, azimuths, has been constructed by us.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 33).
instruments.accuracy: minute divided in four → read to 15″
instruments.principle: A quadrant revolving about a vertical pillar carrying an alidade and sight; swung in azimuth onto the star, the altitude reads directly on the arc and the bearing on a surrounding azimuth ring. With it Tycho fixed the meridian (true north) by averaging Polaris's east- and west-most positions.

Blaeu describes the rotating azimuthal quadrant in Stjerneborg's chamber D. The quadrant turns on its azimuth circle to face any direction, enabling simultaneous measurement of both altitude and azimuth. The coloured illustration shows the instrument in its circular pit with a plumb-bob weight for levelling.

instruments.label: Revolving steel quadrant
instruments.material: a circle-quadrant braced inside a rigid steel square
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: A revolving quadrant built in steel (1588) for rigidity and precision, and the physically largest of Tycho's quadrants (radius 194 cm per Wolfschmidt 2002; Thoren gives 'one and three-quarters metres'). It was actually the old Q. max — the 5-cubit steel quadrant inaugurated 21 March 1581, Tycho's first Hven-shop instrument, which had to be abandoned due to unstable pillars — recycled into useful form after being given a completely stable base (Thoren, p. 177). Braced inside a rigid steel square and turning on a vertical iron axle, it was so solidly built that — Tycho records — a man could hang on it and ride it round several turns without disturbing it. Among the latest of the Stjerneborg battery. Not extant. The Mechanica delineates this quadrant twice: as Fig. 7 (p. 37), revolving in a brick crypt about a steel axis, and again as Fig. 21 (p. 93) in its earlier mounting on a steel azimuth-horizon carried by five columns — Tycho noting it had already been 'described … among the instruments delineated under No. 7'. In his own words: “This quadrant, which is entirely made of solid steel, and further surrounded with a steel square, serves the same purpose as the previous one, with even greater accuracy, since it is considerably larger.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 37).
instruments.principle: A circle-quadrant braced inside a steel square, turnable about a vertical iron axle; the alidade reads altitude on the arc while rules carry the bearing to a c. 350 cm azimuth ring. So solidly built that — Tycho records — a man could hang on it and ride it round several turns without disturbing it.

instruments.label: Great equatorial armillary sphere
instruments.dimensions: one complete revolving armilla seven cubits in diameter — Tycho's own figure, ≈272 cm (radius ≈136 cm); a fixed nine-cubit (≈350 cm) semicircular armilla (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 14, p. 65)
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: The great equatorial armillary of the Stjerneborg crypt, 1.36 m radius (Wolfschmidt 2002; Thoren: 'one-and-a-third metre'), completed by the summer solstice of 1585 — the single most important instrument on Hven (Thoren, ch. 5, p. 174). Foundation laid December 1584. Its single declination ring — made of wood to minimise flexure, except for brass alidades and graduation strips — was pivoted on a hollow steel axis tilted to the Hven latitude. In simplicity it rivalled the mural quadrant; right ascension and declination are read directly, in the equatorial coordinate system astronomers still use. Tycho had tried a zodiacal (ecliptic) armillary first but abandoned it almost immediately; the converted zodiacal armillary was the first equatorial armillary (c. 1583–84), the two smaller equatorial armillaries in the Uraniborg castle itself (north and south, 1584) were the second step, and this great Stjerneborg instrument was the third and culminating form: 'a third, which was to become the single most important instrument on Hven' (Thoren, p. 174). After 1585, the great armillary and the revolving quadrant together enabled Tycho to cross-check the mural quadrant systematically, and it was by this comet-of-1585 season that he achieved his 1′ accuracy target (Thoren, p. 190). Not extant. In his own words: “It has one complete armilla [ring] only which can revolve, and another semicircular one, which is fixed.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 65).
instruments.accuracy: ≈¼′ — one of his most accurate instruments
instruments.principle: A single great declination ring whose axle is set parallel to the Earth's axis (tilted to Stjerneborg's latitude). Because that axis is the polar axis, a sight swung onto a star reads its declination directly on the ring and its hour angle on the equatorial arc below; right-ascension differences between a known and an unknown star are read on the same arc.

instruments.label: Zodiacal (ecliptic) armillary sphere
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: A zodiacal (ecliptic) armillary, measuring celestial longitudes and latitudes in the traditional Ptolemaic system of ecliptic coordinates. Tycho's initial zodiacal armillary (ca. 1583) was tried and abandoned almost immediately — 'he seems to have decided so quickly that the zodiacal form of the armillary would not work that he did not bother to record any observations made with it until after he had converted it to equatorial form' (Thoren, p. 174) — and the conversion to equatorial form constituted his invention of the equatorial armillary. The Mechanica plate (V, 72–87) shows a later, mature zodiacal instrument, grouped by Thoren under 1585. Tycho kept it for its traditional role (solar-longitude measurements) but regarded the equatorial type as his real instrument. Not extant. In his own words: “This instrument consists of four armillae [rings] only (while my predecessors used five or six).” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 53).
instruments.dimensions: four armillae; steel meridian ring three cubits in diameter — Tycho's own figure, ≈117 cm (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 11, p. 53)
instruments.principle: Four rings representing ecliptic great circles, the outer a steel meridian carrying the polar axis. The ecliptic ring is turned onto a star of known longitude to orient the sphere, after which celestial latitude and longitude are read directly — the traditional Ptolemaic type Tycho kept but judged cumbersome (the rings, he complained, were too heavy).

instruments.label: Astronomical sextant with parallel-slit sights
instruments.date: 1584 at Hven (the design first devised at Augsburg, c. 1569)
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: The astronomical sextant Tycho first devised at Augsburg (c.1569, with Petrus Ramus in mind) and refined at Hven with parallel-slit sights. Its priority — and the parallel-slit sights — are the matter of the Wittich dispute aired in the long 1587 letter to Rothmann: Paul Wittich, after his 1580 visit to Hven, reproduced Tycho's instruments at the Landgrave's observatory in Kassel. Not extant. In his own words: “The astronomical sextant instrument, which is particularly convenient in use, was first invented by myself, about twenty years ago.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 25).
instruments.material: wood clad in brass; brass limb, alidade and sights
instruments.principle: A 60° star-distance sextant on a ball-and-socket copper globe so it can be turned into the plane of any two stars. One observer holds the fixed sight on one star, a second moves the alidade onto the other, both aiming at a central cylinder; the arc between reads the distance. For very small gaps a detached parallel sight keeps the two observers from colliding. Fitted with Tycho's pinnacidia (parallel-slit sights).

blaeu.english:
THE SEXTANT, serving for the observation of altitudes: and its construction and use.

Located in the large and southern Observatory of Uraniborg (marked O in the floor plan). Sections I–VI describe the sextant's construction: the two arms forming a 60° arc; the graduated scale; the method using two simultaneous observers; and the verification procedure. Blaeu notes that this is the first instrument Tycho devised and the one from which all his other sextants derived.

instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: An altitude-azimuth half-circle of 233 cm diameter on a 155 cm horizon ring, raised on five stone piers in the larger southern observatory of Uraniborg, surmounted by three figures (Urania, Geometry, Arithmetic). Its sight-rule pivots at one end of the diameter, on the rim; by Euclid's inscribed-angle theorem the angle subtended there is twice the true altitude, so the scale is engraved at double spacing and reads altitude directly, with azimuth on the horizon ring. One of the principal instruments engraved in the Mechanica. Not extant. In his own words: “We have also devised another instrument suitable for accurate measures of altitudes and azimuths, the appearance of which can be seen from the figure.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 41).
instruments.location: larger southern observatory, Uraniborg (on five stone piers)
instruments.principle: An altitude-azimuth half-circle whose sight-rule pivots at the rim, not the centre. By Euclid's inscribed-angle theorem the rim-subtended angle is twice the central angle, so Tycho engraved the altitude scale at double spacing and the rim-pivoted rule then reads true altitude directly; azimuth is read on the north-set horizon ring. Wennberg's aside — 'Tycho knew his Euclid' — is the whole point.

instruments.label: Arcus bipartitus — the bipartite arc (1583)
instruments.description: A distance-measuring arc Tycho invented in 1583, while determining the precise positions of the stars in Cassiopeia for the new-star discussion of the Progymnasmata. On the ordinary sextant two observers had to sight the same small interstellar gap and got in each other's way; the bipartite arc solved this by splitting the axis of the measured angle into two parallel 'zero points'. Constructing it, Tycho realised the same split-axis principle could be adapted to the sextant itself — so the instrument is as much a step in the evolution of his sextant design as an instrument in its own right (Thoren, Lord of Uraniborg, pp. 169–170, Fig. 5.13; TBOO V, 68–71). Enumerated among the Mechanica instruments. Not extant. In his own words: “… an instrument which can measure smaller distances up to one-twelfth of the circumference of the circle, or, as it is called, one sign of the zodiac.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 69).
instruments.dimensions: alidade four cubits long — Tycho's own figure, ≈155 cm (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 15, p. 69); measures up to one-twelfth of the circle (one zodiac sign)
instruments.principle: A bar carrying two 30° arcs whose zero-points sit mid-scale, and a cross-piece of two cylinders at the arcs' centres. With both sights at zero the two sight-lines are parallel, so two observers see the same (effectively infinitely distant) star; swinging the right sight onto a nearby star reads the small angle — up to 15°, or up to 30° by also shifting the left sight.

instruments.label: Parallactic instrument (triquetrum / regulae)
instruments.fate: destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619
instruments.description: Tycho's parallactic instrument (two triquetra), of the ancient Greek and Copernican type, for measuring zenith distances. In the Mechanica Tycho sets his brass instruments against Copernicus's own fir-wood triquetrum. Not extant. In his own words: “This parallatic instrument, which is also called the Ptolemaic rulers, I have wished to construct, since it requires very few accessories, namely, three rulers, in order to measure in a moment the zenith distance of a star, and hence its altitude.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 45).
instruments.dimensions: three equal rulers, each four cubits — Tycho's own figure, ≈155 cm (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 9, p. 45).
instruments.accuracy: zenith distance on a sine scale
instruments.principle: The ancient 'Ptolemaic rules': two equal hinged rules raised by a cord over a pulley, the whole turnable in azimuth on a central pillar. Turned onto the star and the rules raised onto it, the zenith distance is read at the plumb-line on a specially graduated sine scale; altitude = 90°−z.

THE PARALLACTIC INSTRUMENT; which is in the large northern observatory marked R. Its construction and use.

Blaeu reproduces both the traditional Ptolemaic/Copernican triquetrum (upper) and Tycho’s improved version (lower) on a single comparison plate — unique to Blaeu among the 17th-century sources. instruments.label: Copernicus's triquetrum — the relic from Frauenburg
instruments.material: pine, eight feet long, scaled by pen and ink
instruments.description: A wooden triquetrum (parallactic rulers) reputed to have been made and used by Copernicus himself — the single most celebrated relic in Tycho's collection. When Elias Olsen Morsing returned from his 1584 expedition to Frauenburg (Frombork), sent to re-measure the polar altitude that Copernicus had gotten wrong, the cathedral canons — impressed by the expedition and the attention it drew to their illustrious predecessor — sent the instrument back with him as a gift to Tycho. Genuinely awed, Tycho placed it on permanent display in the North Observatory at Uraniborg and composed an impromptu Latin poem to commemorate the occasion (TBOO V, 44–47; partly trans. Edward Rosen in Dobrzycki, ed., Nicholas Copernicus on the Revolutions, 1978, p. 412). His reverence later gave way to objectivity: rulers only eight feet long, made of pine and scaled by pen and ink, could not yield decent observations, and Tycho — though he had already built a larger brass version and found it wanting — duplicated Copernicus's model in his own shop just to test it. Because he circulated the verdict so widely in the Mechanica, Thoren notes the replica 'may well have been the last such instrument built.' Distinct from Tycho's own working parallactic instrument, the brass triquetrum of the north observatory; not extant. Five years on, Tycho summed up Copernicus's instruments: 'by means of these puny cudgels he surmounted the lofty Olympus' (TBOO VI, 253).

Upper portion of Blaeu’s unique dual comparison plate (p. 193), showing the ancient Ptolemaic triquetrum as used by Copernicus — the three hinged rods of the traditional design. Placed opposite Tycho’s improved version on the same sheet, this comparison visualises Tycho’s explicit self-positioning as Copernicus’s methodological successor and reformer.

instruments.label: Globus magnus orichalcicus — the great brass globe
instruments.material: fir-wood shell (commissioned Augsburg 1570 from Christopher Schissler) sheathed in brass
instruments.dimensions: diameter almost six feet — Tycho's own figure, ≈149 cm; on a stand about five feet (≈130 cm) high (Mechanica 1946, Fig. 22, p. 103)
instruments.fate: returned to Copenhagen; destroyed in the University observatory-tower fire of 1728
instruments.description: A celestial globe of almost six Tychonic feet (c. 149 cm) in diameter. Its wooden shell was commissioned in 1570 from Christopher Schissler the Elder, the leading Augsburg instrument-maker, who built it of many fir staves and rings fitted together like a great puzzle (Christianson, On Tycho's Island, p. 358; Dreyer, p. 112). On Tycho's return to Augsburg in 1575 it was found not perfectly spherical and slightly cracked; once received in Denmark in 1576 the cracks were stopped and the sphericity restored, after which the globe was observed over a two-year period to be sure it would hold its shape through the changeable Danish climate before being sheathed in brass, marked with ecliptic and equator divided to a minute of arc, and mounted in divided meridian and horizon rings. An inscription on the horizon dated its completion to 1584; only then were star positions engraved — Tycho's own measured places, added down to 1595 — making it a precision computing instrument as well as a showpiece (Mosley, Bearing the Heavens, ch. 4). The maker of the shell is normally identified as Christopher Schissler the Elder, though Mosley flags the identification as not beyond doubt. The longest-surviving of all Tycho's instruments, with a circuitous return: listed in the 6 Dec 1621 Belvedere inventory ('Ein sehr grosser globus coelestis vom metall'), it was acquired c.1625 by the Jesuit Christoph Scheiner for the Jesuit College at Neisse (Nysa) in Silesia, whence in 1632 it was carried as war-booty to Copenhagen by Prince Ulrik, son of Christian IV; there it stood in the University's observatory tower until that tower and all its contents burned in 1728 (Mortensen, Fra Tycho Brahes Bogsamling). In his own words: “A globe of this size, so solidly and finely worked, and correct in every respect, has never I think been constructed up to now by any man anywhere in the world.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 104).
instruments.accuracy: ecliptic & equator divided by transversals to 1′; >1000 stars
instruments.principle: A precision celestial globe used as an analogue computer: set the pole-altitude on the meridian at the horizon, turn a star to the meridian to read its declination there and its right ascension on the equator; a movable vertical circle gives altitude and the horizon ring azimuth — all four coordinates, and the conversions between the three systems.

instruments.label: Horologia — the observatory clocks
instruments.description: The mechanical clocks kept for timing observations — unreliable in the period, which is why Tycho cross-checked time by his Mechanical-Equator method rather than trusting the clocks alone. They went with the rest of the apparatus to Bohemia and were among the instruments the Emperor purchased after Tycho's death: Kepler used one of Tycho's clocks to observe the lunar eclipses of December 1601 and May 1603 (Dreyer, p. 365). Not extant. In his own words: “We have at our disposal four such clocks. One of these, the largest, manages the whole business with the aid of three wheels, of which the largest, cast from solid pure brass, has 1200 teeth. The diameter of this wheel is two cubits [≈78 cm]. The three other clocks are smaller, and need more wheels.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 30).
instruments.accuracy: unreliable — Tycho preferred to derive time from measured hour angles
instruments.principle: Mechanical clocks (one with a 78 cm wheel of 1200 teeth) for timing transits; Tycho distrusted them, also tried mercury- and lead-oxide outflow clocks, and in practice fixed the time from the Sun's or a star's measured hour angle (e.g. on the great equatorial armilla).
instruments.dimensions: four clocks; the largest driven by a 1200-tooth solid-brass wheel two cubits (≈78 cm) across — Tycho's own account (Mechanica 1946, p. 30)

instruments.label: Smaller iron sextant (Bürgi c.1600 / disputed) — surviving
instruments.institution: Národní technické muzeum (National Technical Museum), Prague
instruments.maker: Jost Bürgi (1552–1632) per Šíma 1993 / Wolfschmidt 2002; or Pater Johann Klein (18th c.) per Weinek 1901 / Mortensen
instruments.dimensions: iron; radius 1.11 m
instruments.description: The smaller ('Nr. 5') of the two iron sextants in the Národní technické muzeum, Prague — radius 1.11 m. Its maker is genuinely disputed. Modern scholarship (Šíma 1993; Wolfschmidt 2002) attributes it to the celebrated clockmaker and instrument-maker Jost Bürgi (1552–1632) of the Prague years, grouping it with the Habermel sextant as the only surviving instruments associated with Tycho. The older Weinek 1901 / Mortensen reading instead held it 'probably made by Pater Johann Klein', director of Prague's Mathematical Chamber 1732–82 — i.e. an 18th-century instrument, not Tychonic at all (the c.1780 inventory's claim that it was 'a smaller sextant of Tycho Brahe, which he brought to Prague' notwithstanding). A sextant of the same size and very similar form survives at the Kremsmünster observatory in Austria, described by Rankl 1946 as 'Der Tychonische Sextant (von Bürgi)'. That Tycho's own Hven instruments are all lost makes any Prague-period survivor precious; the Bürgi attribution is the current consensus but graded B for the open dispute. For the shared Belvedere → Kunstkammer → 1648-Armoury → Herget (1782) → NTM Prague provenance of both surviving sextants, see Fučíková 2002 (detailed under the Habermel sextant).
instruments.principle: A 60° iron star-distance sextant of the Prague years.

instruments.label: Sextant by Erasmus Habermel (1600) — surviving
instruments.institution: Národní technické muzeum (National Technical Museum), Prague
instruments.maker: Erasmus Habermel (b. Nuremberg c.1538, d. Prague 1606)
instruments.dimensions: iron; radius 1.295 m (to the middle of the graduated arc)
instruments.inscription: on the alidade: 'Pragae fecit Erasm. Habermel 1600'
instruments.description: An iron sextant of 1.295 m radius (measured to the middle of the graduated arc), its alidade signed 'Pragae fecit Erasm. Habermel 1600', made by Erasmus Habermel (b. Nuremberg c.1538, d. Prague 1606), the leading instrument-maker at Rudolf II's court. It survives in the Národní technické muzeum, Prague, the larger ('Nr. 4') of the two iron sextants the Prague observatory has long shown as Tycho's (the c.1780 inventory: 'Ein grosser Sextant von Tycho Brahe, der im Jahre 1600 von Erasmus Habermel verfertigt wurde'). Modern scholarship (Šíma 1993; Wolfschmidt 2002) groups it among the only surviving instruments associated with Tycho's working life — everything from Hven is lost. Whether Tycho himself owned or used it is, however, contested: Wolfschmidt calls the two survivors 'so-called Tychonic sextants (but actually made by Bürgi and Habermel)', and the older Weinek 1901 / Mortensen reading thought it 'hardly probable' that Tycho owned this sextant — its construction stands well behind the Mechanica instruments — suggesting instead a Hoffmann→Kepler provenance (one of the instruments Baron Hoffmann lent Kepler when use of the Tychonic instruments was denied him). Hence: existence and maker A (inscription-certain); the attribution to Tycho's own observatory graded B. Later provenance is now traceable (Fučíková 2002): both sextants stood among Rudolf II's instruments at the Prague Belvedere / Kunstkammer (a large instrument there was valued at 600 in the 1619 catalogue, vs 40–80 × three-score groschen for the rest); they proved too large for the Swedish removal of 1648 and were left in the Castle Armoury (1650 inventory), sold at Joseph II's 1782 auction to Franz Leonard Herget (public teacher of mechanics/hydraulics), and eventually passed to the Národní technické muzeum — Fučíková argues they never left Prague.
instruments.principle: A 60° iron star-distance sextant; the alidade signed by Habermel, 1600.

instruments.label: Sextant of Herrevadskloster — the new-star sextant
instruments.location: Herrevadskloster, Skåne (his uncle Steen Bille's house)
instruments.dimensions: two 155 cm legs, hinged
instruments.material: walnut clad in copper; copper arc and central sight
instruments.accuracy: arc divided to single degrees and minutes (1° ≈ 24 mm, 1′ ≈ ½ mm)
instruments.principle: A 60° star-distance sextant: a fixed copper sight at the centre, the moving leg locked and fine-adjusted by a screw against an inner arc; sighting along both legs gives the angle between two stars.
instruments.description: The sextant Tycho had made at Herrevadskloster — the instrument with which, in November 1572, he measured the new star (SN 1572) in Cassiopeia: its distances to the nine brightest stars of the constellation, and (the star being circumpolar and culminating too near the zenith to reach) its lowest meridian altitude, 27°45′, taken by laying the sextant on a window-frame and levelling it with a plumb-line. These are the observations behind De nova stella (1573). Later judged obsolete; superseded by the Hven sextants. Not extant. The Mechanica does not tie this instrument to Herrevad by name, but by Tycho's own account it is the sextant he “had made” to measure the 1572 new star: its distance-form is engraved as Fig. 18 (whose plate is dated 1572) and its altitude-mounting — the configuration illustrated here — as Fig. 19 (p. 85). The half-sextant for small angles, catalogued separately, is that same Fig. 18 instrument, so the two entries may describe one physical sextant. In his own words: “In this fashion I measured the minimum altitude of the new star which was seen in the year 1572 and the following year, as it passed the meridian below the pole.” (Mechanica, trans. Raeder, Strömgren & Strömgren 1946, p. 85).

instruments.description: Tycho's earliest and smallest quadrant (radius ≈39 cm), of gilt brass, for altitudes. It is best remembered for a small allegorical painting on it: a tree green and living on the left, dead and withered on the right; beneath the living branches a youth with laurel, book and star-globe, beneath the dead a skeleton reaching for a table of riches — with a Latin verse that only study and knowledge confer immortality. Later kept at Stjerneborg. Not extant. In his own words: “The use of this quadrant is for finding the altitudes of the stars and of the sun and moon in such cases when complete accuracy is not necessary, a value with an error less than two or three minutes being sufficient.” (Mechanica, trans. techniques.name: The transversal (diagonal) scale
techniques.summary: Tycho's signature precision device — a band of diagonal lines crossing a ladder of parallel rows that turns a coarse degree-scale into a reading good to a single arcminute, and to c. 10″ on his largest arcs, by interpolating diagonally. He first saw the idea in Leipzig as a youth and perfected it; it is the chief reason his instruments out-resolved every predecessor.

techniques.name: Pinnacidia — parallel-slit sights
techniques.summary: Tycho's own sighting device: two equal parallel squares with adjustable brass slits, so the eye lines the star up through four slits at once — removing the parallax of the eye and letting the slit be matched to a star's brightness. It is the 'sight a central cylinder' instruction that recurs across the armillae and sextants.

techniques.name: The Nonius (Nunes) scale — and why Tycho dropped it
techniques.summary: Before the transversal, fine readings were attempted with the auxiliary-arc system of the Portuguese mathematician Pedro Nunes (Latin Nonius). Tycho fitted it to his smallest and medium quadrants and one sextant, but found the many nested arcs near-impossible to engrave accurately, and abandoned it for his transversal division.

techniques.name: Reading the sky in equatorial coordinates
techniques.summary: Tycho's conceptual innovation as much as a mechanical one: orienting an armillary's axis parallel to the Earth's axis so a single ring reads declination and hour angle (and right-ascension differences) directly — the equatorial system astronomers still use — instead of the traditional ecliptic (zodiacal) armillary's latitude and longitude.

techniques.name: Mounting in the meridian
techniques.summary: Fixing a great arc exactly in the north–south meridian plane turns 'measure an altitude' into 'measure the meridian altitude', from which declination and latitude follow by simple addition or subtraction. Combined with rigidity — stone piers, steel frames, the underground Stjerneborg crypts — this is what made the precision real over long observing runs.

problems.q: the height of a body above the horizon
problems.principle: A quarter-circle graduated from 0° at the top to 90° on a plumb-line reads a star's height above the horizon directly.
Two arms sighting from a single vertex over a graduated arc give the angle between two points — with no horizon needed.

problems.q: right ascension and declination, in the sky's own frame
problems.principle: A ring set parallel to the celestial equator hands you declination directly; a second gives right ascension — no computation.

problems.q: longitude and latitude on the ecliptic
problems.principle: Rings aligned to the zodiac read a body's longitude and latitude in the ecliptic coordinates the ancients used.

problems.q: the angular distance of a body from the zenith
problems.principle: Two hinged rulers — the ancient Ptolemaic method Copernicus still used; Tycho built his own in brass, then moved beyond it.

singleton_band.label: Also — outside the five problems
singleton_band.note: The great celestial globe: not a measuring instrument at all, but a physical model of the whole sky on which Tycho plotted the 1000-plus stars his instruments had fixed. He did not design it — the brass-covered wooden shell was made by Christopher Schissler of Augsburg (1570) — but he completed and engraved it, so it belongs in the Mechanica and here.

desiderata.title: The instruments Tycho did not engrave
desiderata.text: Chapter 25 of the Mechanica ('on certain other instruments of ours not yet engraved', TBOO V, 96–101) names a fork-shaped sextant with 155 cm arms of Brazil wood, a large semicircle for distances beyond a sixth of the circle, an astronomical radius, an astronomical ring, a portable armilla of 60 cm radius and an astrolabe, and promises more. Thoren's chart adds an Icelandic quadrant (1589) and a camera-obscura 'canal' (1591), and separates a 'semicirculus' of 1588 that he suspects is the azimuth semicircle under another pivot. None of these has a record here; the edition models the engraved instruments and five documented others.

desiderata.title: The instruments of the student and Augsburg years
desiderata.text: Thoren's chart opens with a half-sextant of 1569; the sextant Tycho left with Paul Hainzel, the Basel quadrants of 1568 and the gilt quadrant by Steffen Brenner used at the eclipse of 8 December 1573 are recorded, as objects of a stay, in Loca. Only the great Augsburg quadrant and the student cross-staff have records here.

desiderata.title: One sextant or two
desiderata.text: The Herrevad sextant that measured the new star and the 'half-sextant for small angles' of the Mechanica (Fig. 18, whose plate is dated 1572) may be one physical instrument, engraved in its distance form as Fig. 18 and in its altitude mounting as Fig. 19. The two entries are kept and counted as one object; the merge is the owner's decision.

desiderata.title: Dates not yet reconciled with Thoren 1973
desiderata.text: The dates follow Wennberg 2007, the 1946 translation and Thoren 1990. Thoren's chart differs for the steel sextant (1576 against 1574 here), the brass azimuthal quadrant (1583 against 1576), the medium quadrant (1577 against 1580, though his own figure caption says 1580) and the zodiacal armillary (1581 against c. 1583–85). His 1973 article, which redates several instruments from the observation logs, has not been read for this edition.

desiderata.title: The maker of the smaller Prague sextant
desiderata.text: Bürgi (Šíma 1993, Wolfschmidt 2002) or Johann Klein, the eighteenth-century director of the Prague mathematical chamber (Weinek 1901, Mortensen 1942). The Kremsmünster sextant of the same size and form is the comparandum. Šíma's article has not been read in full.

desiderata.title: Whether Tycho owned either surviving sextant
desiderata.text: Mortensen thought it 'hardly probable' that Tycho owned the Habermel sextant and proposed a Hoffmann–Kepler provenance instead; Wolfschmidt calls both 'so-called Tychonic'. The grades record the existence and maker as secure and the link to Tycho as probable at best.

desiderata.title: No museum object records located
desiderata.text: The National Technical Museum's own object records for the two sextants have not been found online; the inventory numbers here (Nos. 4 and 5) are those of the observatory's c. 1780 inventory as reported by Mortensen.

desiderata.title: A folio locus for every plate
desiderata.text: The plates are reproduced from the Royal Library's copy 2; the copy online is copy 1. No page-level concordance between the two has been made, and the plates carry no signature or folio reference into the unpaginated 1598 book (Mortensen cites it by folio: 'Fol. H. 2').

desiderata.title: The clocks
desiderata.text: Tycho names four clocks; they are one record. Their placement is collective (the mural-quadrant room at Uraniborg, the warming room at Stjerneborg) and no individual clock is described beyond the largest, with its 1200-tooth wheel.

desiderata.title: The destruction of the Hven instruments
desiderata.text: 'Destroyed in the aftermath of the Bohemian war of 1619' is a collective statement (Gassendi, followed by Dreyer and Wolfschmidt); Mortensen shows the 1621 inventory still listing a quadrant 'with many appurtenant instruments' at the Belvedere, and a 1672 report that the instruments had 'long since been sold to brass-founders'. No individual instrument's end is dated except the Augsburg quadrant (1574) and the globe (1728).

transmission.event: Tycho leaves Hven; the instruments follow him into exile and, in 1599, to Bohemia.
Tycho arrives in Prague and lodges in the Curtius house; at his audience the Emperor asks him to send for the instruments still on their way.
The great instruments from Hven arrive and are set up, at the Emperor's wish, in the Belvedere in the castle garden (Tycho to Magini, 24 January 1601); Tycho observes there from 2 December 1600.
All the instruments are moved from the Belvedere to the Curtius house and observation resumes.
Tycho dies; Kepler closes the observation journal with the account of his illness and death.

The Emperor secures the observations and instruments from the heirs, who had asked 100,000 thalers, for 20,000 at six per cent; 4,000 are paid in 1602 and 1,000 in 1608, and nothing after. The claim was still unsettled in 1671.
Kepler, denied the use of the instruments, which are stored in a cellar under the Curtius house, is lent a quadrant and a sextant by Baron J. F. Hoffmann.
An imperial order to Kepler to pack the instruments and send them to Vienna 'for greater safety'; apparently not carried out.
An imperial rescript on the heirs' claim states that the instruments and books 'remain in this Crown of Bohemia'. When the Curtius house changes hands the instruments return to the Belvedere.

Destruction in the disturbances that followed the death of Emperor Matthias, when Prague was held for Frederick of the Palatinate: some instruments converted to other uses, the rest destroyed or dispersed (Gassendi, Vita, 1655, p. 216). The version that attaches the loss to the battle of the White Mountain, 8 November 1620, is a misreading of Gassendi.
The inventory of the Prague treasury and Kunstkammer still lists, in the Belvedere, 'no. 1424, a very large celestial globe of metal' and 'no. 1425, a quadrant with many appurtenant instruments'.
The globe is acquired by Christoph Scheiner for the Jesuit college at Neisse in Silesia.
Prince Ulrik, son of Christian IV, takes the globe from Neisse as war booty to Copenhagen, where it is placed in the observatory of the Round Tower.
The Swedish removal of Rudolf II's collections leaves the two large iron sextants behind; the Castle Armoury inventory of 1650 lists them.
The English legation secretary Henshaw reports that 'Tycho Brahe's instruments were long ago sold to brass-founders'.
The globe burns in the Round Tower fire; the wooden body is consumed and the brass melts, leaving some lumps, the meridian ring, iron rings and the axle, since lost.

The Prague observatory's earliest inventory lists 'No. 4, a large sextant of Tycho Brahe, made in the year 1600 by Erasmus Habermel' and 'No. 5, a smaller sextant of Tycho Brahe, which he brought with him to Prague'.
At Joseph II's auction of the Castle collections the two sextants are sold to Franz Leonard Herget, public teacher of mechanics and hydraulics.

The Prague observatory sells discarded instruments; the 'Tychonic' pieces among them, a sundial inscribed 'Insula Heveen A.D. 1578' and a planetarium engraved 'Ty. de Brahe', are forgeries, bought by the painter Gabriel Max and given in 1909 to the Deutsches Museum in Munich.
Weinek publishes the two Prague sextants, with plates.
The two sextants pass to the Národní technické muzeum, Prague, where they are displayed.
